Converts aldehydes to carboxylic acids, aromatic and quaternary azaheterocyclic compounds to lactams, typically by using molecular oxygen as the terminal electron acceptor and producing hydrogen peroxide as a by-product (PubMed:10190983, PubMed:10377246, PubMed:19401776, PubMed:23462233, PubMed:4256441). Under some conditions, especially with electron-deficient substrates or limited oxygen, can also catalyze reduction reactions using N-methylnicotinamide, 2-hydroxypyrimidine or benzaldehyde as electron donor substrate (PubMed:15720138, PubMed:23462233). These reductive activities include N-O bond reductions in nitro groups (e.g., imidacloprid, IMI), hydroxamic acids, and oxazoles (e.g., zonisamide), as well as N-S bond reductions of sulfoxides (e.g., sulindac) (By similarity)

In contrast to the NAD-dependent reaction, the NADP-dependent reaction does not follow classical Michaelis-Menten kinetics. The saturation kinetics of the NADP-dependent reaction shows an unexpectedly bumpy curve with several more or less pronounced intermediate plateaus, which can be explained by the assumption that the catalytic or binding constants first decrease, then increase with saturation. The first saturation phase is characterized by negative cooperativity. The later saturation phases display sigmoidal shapes indicating positive cooperativity.
